# Preface.

Since humans have lived upon the earth, perhaps no age has been as remarkable as our own, in which things are converging that have rarely been seen together in such diversity and abundance. Without even mentioning the striking revolutions—which perhaps appear as a prelude to a great <term>palingenesis</term> <note>From the Greek *palin* (again) and *genesis* (birth); this term refers to a doctrine of rebirth or world-renewal, often used in 18th-century philosophy to describe a total spiritual or physical transformation of the human race.</note> of the earth and the human race within the realms of nature and morality—this age distinguishes itself particularly through the opposing—

# Preface.

—firmest teachings, opinions, systems, and activities. Truth and error, light and darkness, play and seriousness appear as nothing but counterpoints. The purest as well as the most depraved <term>way of thinking</term> <note>Original: *Denkungsart*; a common 18th-century term for a person’s mindset or intellectual character.</note> are equally prevalent; the lowest and most sublime principles run alongside and against one another. Should the time not already be approaching, however, when a spirit from above—as living as it is two-edged—will penetrate the marrow and bone of the human race and bring about a great separation? <note>This is a clear allusion to the New Testament (Hebrews 4:12), which describes the word of God as a "two-edged sword" piercing even to the "marrow and bone." The author is suggesting a coming moment of divine judgment or spiritual clarity.</note>

While materialism and atheism still have their numerous aspirants, others build in deep silence and under the gentle influences of a steady light upon a temple of the Eternal Spirit, which can outlast more than one world. While so many of our contemporaries, incapable of true reflection, prefer to choose every appearance and shimmer rather than feeling the desire and calling for serious investigations into the <term>highest concern of humanity</term>, <note>In the context of 18th-century religious philosophy, the "highest concern" usually refers to the immortality of the soul and the relationship between the human and the divine.</note>

<summary>The author characterizes his era as a chaotic clash of opposing values—truth versus error and materialism versus spirituality. He anticipates a forthcoming spiritual "separation" where a divine influence will distinguish between those lost in superficiality and those building a lasting "temple of the Spirit."</summary>

<keywords>Counterpoints, Materialism, Atheism, Eternal Spirit, Spiritual Crisis, Enlightenment Philosophy, Biblical Allusion</keywords>

...[seek], there are, on the contrary, others who recognize points of rest only in the most secret and hidden depths of things—resting places that are worthy of the immortal human being. While some of our <term>scholars</term> <note>Original: *Schriftgelehrten*; literally "those learned in the Scriptures." In this period, it often carried a pejorative tone, referring to theologians who focus on the "letter" of the law rather than its spiritual "spirit."</note> turn the almost lost spirit of the Scripture into the most changeable shell of earthly trivialities, so that it does not appear as if anything remains hidden in the sanctuary for which they have no sense, and so that they may all the more conveniently serve the <term>god of this world</term> <note>A biblical allusion to 2 Corinthians 4:4, usually referring to worldly interests, vanity, or even the devil, as opposed to the divine.</note> and political vanity, others open a holy perspective. In this view, even the most sublime truths appear in full clarity and harmony, refreshing the languishing earth like a balsamic dew from above. If the former must make the holy commonplace and degrade the divine in order to bring it into balance with their own lowly thoughts, the latter demonstrate a true wisdom, beauty, and strength of the divine from within itself, as well as its harmony with the forgotten—

VIII

-> Preface. <-

...the teachings not only of this school, but of this system in general, are presented completely, purely, and worthily. Their content, or the <term>science</term> <note>Original: *Wissenschaft*; in the 18th-century context, this refers to a systematic body of knowledge or a rigorous philosophical framework, rather than the modern experimental sciences.</note> upon which it is based, cannot, given the actual state of affairs, claim general applause; however, it remains what it is, without deserving contempt. A large part of it is based on the <term>laws of nature</term> <note>Original: *Gesetze der Natur*; likely referring to the spiritual and "natural" laws of the universe as understood in theosophy or Martinism.</note>, which are not fabricated, and on sources of knowledge that are somewhat more than "impure puddles." 

Even if certain fundamental doctrines of this system contained less truth than they actually do, one should still wish that they were true, because the benefit of their application must be obvious to every thinking person. They resolve difficulties which the <term>common sciences</term> <note>Original: *gemeinen Wissenschaften*; referring to the traditional academic and secular disciplines of the Enlightenment which the author finds insufficient for spiritual questions.</note> are not sufficient to resolve; indeed, what is more, they bring to life much that is dead, harmonize the discordant, give all human powers something to do, open a very wide field for the most beneficial activity, and finally show the most sublime goal of the...

-> Preface. <-

...struggle and of the reward in the distance. This very all-encompassing and uplifting nature is one of the primary advantages through which this and similar systems become powerful tools for noble individuals.

Regarding the personal circumstances of the author—or rather, the authors—of the cited works and their society, I wish to say nothing *). They are not **circumcised in the flesh** <note>Original: *Beschnittene am Fleisch*; a biblical allusion (Romans 2:28-29) meaning those who focus only on outward ritual. B. with—

*) Yet I can assure this much from a reliable source: that there are now two secret societies in France, one of which names itself after **St. M—** <note>Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin (1743–1803), the "Unknown Philosopher" whose mystical system, Martinism, focused on the internal "reintegration" of humanity.</note> and the other after **Ch—** <note>Likely refers to the *Chevaliers Bienfaisants de la Cité Sainte* (Beneficent Knights of the Holy City) or perhaps Jacques Cazotte.</note>. Regarding the latter, one may think this way or that with good reason; concerning the former, however, to which our authors belong, the situation is all the better. Both, however, with regard to higher doctrines, constitute the dominant parties in France.

XII

-> ### Preface. <-

Since our unknown authors <note>Refers to the "Unknown Philosophers" (*Philosophes Inconnus*), a title used by the followers of the French mystic Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin.</note> know the value of common knowledge and what can be achieved through it so well—to the extent that even the most famous discoveries of modern times are not foreign to them—then their dissatisfaction with common scientific methods must surely be based on something more than pure ignorance. They must see by a light in which everything counts for what it is worth, but which itself reaches further,

...spoken in earnest, they have done so. One should therefore not have attacked the good Mr. Cl. <note>Abbreviation for Matthias Claudius (1740–1815), the prominent German poet and journalist who published the German translation of Saint-Martin's work in 1782.</note> in such a strutting and scornful manner, as if he must have translated his original entirely incorrectly simply because of the aforementioned circumstance. He certainly has not! Rather, I doubt whether many could be found who, taken as a whole, could have translated it as well as he did. Furthermore, Mr. Cl. possesses such good feeling and striking power of judgment that he does not easily fall into the temptation of mistaking an **Abaddon** <note>A biblical name for the "Destroyer" or an angel of the abyss; the author is arguing that Claudius is too perceptive to be deceived by evil disguised as good.</note> for an **angel of light**, as soon as he occupies himself with the same **by profession** <note>original: *ex professo*</note>. In short, the whole rumor of Jesuitry is a miserable trifle **and nothing more** <note>original: *praetereaque nihil*</note>. —

They also know very well why their teaching can arouse the attention of only a very few in this thinking age, and yet they preferred to make themselves known now, *while spirits are in ferment* <note>original: *où les esprits fermentent*</note>, rather than later.

Moreover, they recommend themselves through the excellent qualities of the heart, of which both writings—especially the *Tableau* <note>Refers to Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin's *Tableau naturel des rapports qui existent entre Dieu, l'homme et l'univers* (A Natural Table of the Relations between God, Man, and the Universe), published in 1782.</note>—give the most undeniable proof. XIV

-> ### Preface. <-

proves: then this should move every ignorant critic <term>critic: *Beurtheiler*, one who evaluates or judges a work</term> and reviewer more to reflection and silence than to disparagement. Who would not know that one can sin greatly even through reviews <note>original: *Recensionen*</note>? Regarding the specific arrangement and purpose of the present writing, the first part contains everything that is essential to the system of the **Unknown Philosophers**, insofar as they have presented it in the two aforementioned works, but in a different order than they themselves employed. This was done not merely because their arrangement seemed inconvenient to many readers, but also because I wished to condense their entire content into a few short sheets. To this end, that which appears scattered in several places concerning the same subjects had to be collected and brought under certain main articles. In this way, the reader is enabled to survey the entire system of our authors with a steady gaze, as well as to judge the unique characteristics of their teachings according to their true relationship. Certain matters have received more light through this simple juxtaposition than they possessed in the original writings

The entire world-system of our theosophists <note>A term for mystical philosophers who seek direct knowledge of the divine; in this context, it likely refers to the school of Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin</note> rests upon the threefold division into the Divine, the Intellectual, and the Sensible <note>original: "das Göttliche, Intellectuelle und Sinnliche"; these represent the realm of God, the realm of pure thought or spirit, and the realm of physical matter experienced through the senses</note>. Every being has its own particular **principle** <note>original Latin: *principium*</note> through which it exists and exerts its power (I, 82–90).

39) There is an invisible, uncontainable **primal fire** <term>Primal Fire: (French: *feu principe*) The foundational spiritual energy or "first fire" from which all physical matter originates in this mystical system.</term>, from which all the particular substances that constitute bodies originate. ### III.
# Humanity.

What our theosophists <term>theosophists: practitioners of a mystical philosophy seeking direct knowledge of the divine, often through the study of nature and internal revelation</term> teach about man in his full scope—namely, concerning his exalted origin, his current state, and his future destiny—is so unique and contains so much that is remarkable and, in part, highly valuable and incomparable, that I consider it all the more necessary to present every essential point found in their two writings regarding this in this section, specifically under the following articles: 1) man in his origin; 2) in his degradation, trial, reconciliation, and restoration; 3) in his social and political state.

### 1. Man in His Origin.

A great revolution in the spirit realm <note>original: *Geisterreich*</note>, by which the absolute sovereignty of the Unity was weakened, seemingly prompted the Being of beings <term>Being of beings: a philosophical name for God as the source from which all other beings emanate</term> to an immediate emanation of himself, in order to [restore] the weakened harmony of the most perfect accord [the]—

<summary>This page introduces a detailed section on the theosophical view of humanity, outlining a three-part study of human origins, the Fall and restoration, and social existence. It begins by describing a "revolution in the spirit realm" that necessitated the creation of man as an emanation of the Divine.</summary>
<keywords>humanity, theosophy, divine origin, emanation, spirit realm, restoration, Being of beings</keywords>

### 2. Man in His Humiliation, Testing, Reconciliation, and Restoration.

But since man, for his **restoration** <note>original: *Wiederherstellung*; a technical term in this philosophy referring to the "Reintegration" of beings into their original divine source.</note>, can do little besides **endure and abstain** <note>original: *επεχε και απεχε* (epéche kai apéche); a Stoic maxim from Epictetus meaning "bear and forbear," or to suffer patiently and practice self-restraint.</note>, these strict demands would lead him more to despair than inspire courage, were there not very secure and powerful means outside of himself to facilitate his **reconciliation** and make his **completion** possible. Furthermore, man himself still possesses enough strength to make use of these gifts from a higher hand, if he only has the courage and will enough to become receptive to them.

Everything here depends on the **higher reaction**, which man in his current state necessarily requires. ### 3. Man in the Social and Political State.

As a **political creature** <term>political creature: From the Greek *zoon politikon*, a concept popularized by Aristotle which suggests that humans are naturally destined to live in organized communities (the *polis*).</term>, man can be considered either according to what he *really* is in this relationship; or according to what he *ought* to be in it. <meta>This page continues from the introduction of the human as a "political creature" on page 77. The catchword at the bottom of the previous page was "to," leading into this discussion on the origins of social structures.</meta>

The origin of society is found neither in the violent rounding up of people by a few over-powerful individuals, nor in the merely arbitrary unions of all individuals into a common whole by means of a **social contract** <note>social contract: A reference to the political theory, popularized by thinkers like Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, suggesting that individuals consent to surrender some freedoms to an authority in exchange for protection of their remaining rights.</note>. These are two common, but highly inadequate and unnatural hypotheses from which people have sought to explain the entire phenomenon of political union. The former shows only sheep for the slaughter and tyrants—and such things did not always exist; the latter, however, presupposes an impossibility which, even if thought of as a reality, would be just as irrational as it would be unjust $^{68}$).

Originally, man was born for **dominion** <note>original: "Herrschaft"</note>, but not over his equals; rather, he was born to rule over lesser beings: consequently

After the **Fall** <note>The biblical "Fall of Man," the transition from a state of innocent obedience to God to a state of guilty disobedience.</note>, some light still remained for humanity. <meta>This page continues the summary of Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin's allegorical interpretations from his work *Tableau naturel*, specifically focusing on his esoteric reading of the opening of the Book of Genesis.</meta>

The phrase "In the beginning" <note>original Hebrew: בראשית (*Bereshit*)</note> refers, in his view, to the divine thought; and "God" <note>original Hebrew: אלהים (*Elohim*)</note> is not the supreme God, but rather designates agents of the second rank who produce the sensory world <note>Saint-Martin, following Martines de Pasqually, believed that the physical world was created by subordinate spiritual beings rather than the primary Godhead.</note> $^{61}$).

The "waters" <note>original Hebrew: מים (*Mayim*)</note> are the invisible original seeds of the universe; and the "spirit of God" <note>original Hebrew: רוח אלהים (*Ruach Elohim*)</note> is the fertilizing action of these agents, just as the meaning of "earth" <note>original Hebrew: ארץ (*Eretz*)</note> designates the actual stage of reconciliation <note>In this mystical tradition, the "reconciliation" is the process by which fallen humanity is restored to its original spiritual status.</note> $^{62}$).

The six symbolic days of creation are an image of the sensory realm and signify the "six united actions that have contributed to material embodiment" <note>original French: *six actions réunies qui ont concouru à la corporisation matérielle*</note>. This same "sixfold order" <note>original Latin: *senarius*</note> is found in the six planets that revolve around their center (7), and is an essential law in mechanics as well as music and ancient chronology; one can also recognize in this just as clearly the two "triads" <note>original Latin: *ternarii*</note> of the action of the earth and the reaction of heaven $^{63}$).

General councils <note>original: "Concilien." ### 3. Mathematics, or the Application of Fundamental Numbers to the Spiritual and Physical Worlds.

True mathematics is something to which all higher sciences are attached; ordinary mathematics, however, is merely a deceptive shadow-image of the true science. Its praised infallibility arises solely from the fact that one makes only material ratios and relationships its subject. As long as one sticks only to these, it certainly cannot err; however, since the true nature of things—which it does not touch at all—is quite different, it will never achieve the purpose of a true science $^{31)}$.

## 1. Nature, Origin, and the Relation of Language to the Nature of Man.

If language and writing are, as the author says, the only two means and attributes through which man reveals his thoughts and powers, then action in general must belong to one of these two; for there are very expressive actions, and word and deed are equally <term>semantic</term> <note>meaningful or communicative; the author suggests that both words and actions function as signs that carry deeper spiritual significance.</note>.

Although the true rights of man lie in speech, no <term>artificial language</term> <note>original: "lingua factitia"; a language created by human convention or invention rather than arising from an internal, natural necessity.</note> shows his true faculty of speech, any more than mere gesturing with signs—such as those used for the speechless—deserves to be called language. This is because such <term>semantics</term>, being based merely on choice and agreement, is not directly grounded in the essence of man; not to mention that it lacks the invaluable quality of **articulation** <note>original: "Ausrede"; here referring to the oral expression or the act of speaking out, which the author considers a divine or essential human gift.</note>. I, 452 = 453.

This is because, without an intellectual foundation, man would be capable neither of receiving such instruction (not even in <term>artificial languages</term> <note>original: "linguis factitiis"; languages created by human convention or invention.</note>) nor of using his organs for rational speech if they were not determined and governed by his intellectual nature. When the author places the origin of language "before time," he is not speaking of artificial languages, which arose within historical time and are a consequence of corrupted sensuality, but of the true, original **spirit-language** <note>original: "Geistsprache"; a primordial mode of communication inherent to the human soul, predating formal grammar and words.</note>, which is as old as the powers of the human spirit itself. In general, regarding everything said here about writing and language, one must maintain a constant regard for the <term>pre- and post-history</term> <note>original: "Vor- und Nachgeschichte"; a reference to the spiritual state of humanity before its current earthly existence and its ultimate destiny afterward.</note> of man.

### 2. Original Language.

There is only one true language for humans, whose signs of expression are just as natural as they are—and must be—universally understandable.

57) I, 463—466. The author does not allow any expression of merely animal sensations and passions to count as language, because he places language solely within the realm of the intellectual. Based on his principles, I would prefer to put it this way: All active beings have the capacity to reveal their powers; there is, therefore, a general <term>semantics</term> <note>In this context, the study of how all things in nature signify or express their internal state.</note> that ascends alongside the levels and powers of the beings themselves. It is either a mere outward manifestation in minerals and vegetables; or, at once, a living expression with sensation and consciousness; or, finally, a speaking revelation in all thinking beings. This last category is again twofold: either purely intellectual among pure spirits, or simultaneously sensory among beings of a dual nature <note>i.e., humans, who possess both a physical body and a spiritual intellect.</note>. In the latter, the sensory is at the same time a proof of the intellectual; it distinguishes itself from the merely animal just as much as the human use of the eyes and ears differs from the animal use of the same.

### VI.

## On Several Primary Symbols and Allegories.

The true understanding of this system rests upon the correct explanation of its allegorical language and certain **symbols**, which can be regarded as its soul and as its fundamental pillars.

Much of this has already been explained in its proper place and on several occasions. However, since a closer evaluation and more precise overview require even more, I deem it good to speak here somewhat more extensively about several points. These shall be: 1) The impenetrable veil or armor of the <term>original human<note>German: 'ursprünglichen Menschen'. In mystical and theosophical traditions, this refers to the 'Adam Kadmon' or the primal, divine state of humanity before the fall into material form.</note></term> along with the fiery, double-edged, and all-penetrating lance granted to him. 2) The forest of seven trees. 3) The allegorical book of ten leaves. 4) The square. 5) The destroyed temple that is to be rebuilt through the <term>Great Work<note>German: 'das grosse Werk'. This is the alchemical 'Magnum Opus', representing the process of spiritual purification and the restoration of the soul to its divine origin.</note></term>. 6) The ineffable name of the Great Being. 7) The sacred names through which life flows to all beings.

### III.

Nothing is more remarkable than that allegorical book of ten leaves, which is discussed in detail in Volume I, page 253 and following. This book—upon the understanding of which rested all the privileges of the glory and luminous nature of the **original man** <note>German: *ursprünglicher Mensch*. This refers to the "ideal" or spiritual human (often called Adam Kadmon in mystical traditions) before the fall into a physical body.</note>—is the great tablet of all beings, the **All** <note>original Greek: ΠΑΝ (*Pan*)</note> or the fullness of all that is, has been, and will be; it is called a "book" because the author refers to the characters, numbers, and forms of beings as the writing and language of God and of Nature. The leaves of that book are its individual parts or divisions, and the fact that there are ten of them stems from the significance of this number, which expresses the fullness or the **plenitude** <note>original Greek: πληρωμα (*pleroma*), a term often used in Gnostic philosophy to describe the totality of divine powers.</note> of the universe.

The original man read this book all at once—that is, he saw the entirety of things with a single glance; now, he can only laboriously spell it out again, one leaf after another, in order to gradually regain his lost powers. These resemble somewhat the seven <term>Bubuns<note>A reference to "Bhuvans" (Sanskrit: *bhuvana*), meaning worlds or planes of existence in Hindu cosmology. This occurs in the presence of God and the divine light, which accompanies man everywhere. In the light of these eternally burning lamps, Christ walks in the midst as the Supreme and Eternal Priest.

### *The Martinists.*

A completely new sect which, turning its back entirely on the paths opened by sound physics and solid chemistry, and divorcing itself from everything natural history tells us, has plunged into an invisible world that it alone perceives.

The Martinists have adopted the visions of the Swede Swedenborg <note>Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772) was a Swedish scientist and theologian who claimed to have received revelations from the spirit world</note>, who saw angels and spoke to them, and who described to us in cold blood <note>original: *de sang-froid*; here meaning with calm, matter-of-fact detail</note> their dwellings, their writing, and their habits; he who finally saw with his own eyes *the wonders of heaven and hell*.

This sect takes its name from its leader <note>Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin (1743–1803), a French philosopher whose mystical works under the pseudonym "The Unknown Philosopher" founded the tradition of Martinism</note>, the author of the book entitled: *Of Errors and Truth* <note>original: *Des Erreurs et de la Vérité*; published in 1775, this work argued that truth could be found through inner revelation rather than rational observation</note>. This book promises us, like so many others, the evidence and conviction of truths, the search for which occupies the entire universe.

The basis of the system is that man is a degraded being, punished in a material body for prior faults, but that the divine spark <note>original: *rayon divin*; literally "divine ray"</note> he carries within himself can still bring him back to a state of greatness, strength, and light.

What and from where is the doctrine of the Martinists? What should one think of it, and where should it be classified? After I have explained, as far as necessary and as briefly as possible, the relationship of the **Martinist** <note>Referring to the followers of Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin (1743–1803), a French mystic known as "the Unknown Philosopher." His system emphasized the internal "reintegration" of man with the divine.</note> system with the **Hebrew Kabbalah** <note>The ancient Jewish mystical tradition focused on the nature of God and the hidden meanings of the Torah.</note> and **Christian Theosophy** <note>A tradition of mystical philosophy seeking direct, intuitive knowledge of the divine and the secrets of nature.</note>, as well as the foundation and actual content of the latter two, I now wish to touch upon a few specific points of the system of **French Theosophy** before I speak of the relative value of the whole.

Regarding the **hieroglyphic symbols** <note>In this context, the author refers to spiritual or allegorical signs and pictorial codes rather than Egyptian script.</note> and **emblems** under which the primary doctrines of this system are hidden, it has already been mentioned that these belong to the ancient **temple-wisdom** <note>A term often used by esoteric writers to refer to a supposed "primeval revelation" or secret knowledge preserved by ancient priesthoods.</note>. Some of these symbols constitute a part of the Kabbalah, but they can also be found elsewhere. Their application is noble and possesses a profound meaning: the entire emblematic form and presentation not only distinguishes the writings of our theosophists—as mysterious monuments—from all similar works of that name, but these very writings reveal themselves at the same time as the result of multiple eras; they connect both to something that preceded them and to something that still exists.

<meta>This page transitions from the general concept of the Divine "All" to the historical origins of the concept of the "One" (the Monad). It argues that while Pythagoras is often credited with this philosophy, its roots actually lie in much older Egyptian mystery traditions, which influenced all ancient accounts of the origin of the gods (theogonies).</meta>

It is commonly believed that the Sage of Samos <note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BCE), the famous Greek philosopher and mathematician.</note> was the first to consecrate the expression of Unity or the **Monad** <note>original Greek: Μονας (Monas)</note> with this particular meaning. As a **numerical token** <note>original Latin: *tessera arithmetica*</note>, it certainly refers to the sacred doctrine of numbers, with which it seems to be of the same age. However, this was so little a Pythagorean invention that, on the contrary, the sacred numbers of the universe were recognized and revered long before Pythagoras hit upon the idea of looking for wisdom in foreign lands. In Egypt, at least, they constituted one of the sacred sciences of the priesthood. Since Pythagoras enjoyed the instruction of the Egyptian **Mystagogues** <term>Mystagogen: priests who initiated seekers into the secret religious mysteries of ancient Egypt.</term>, his symbolic doctrine of numbers—like many of his riddles—seems to have arisen from this source.

Moreover, the **theogonies** <term>Theogonies: systems or stories explaining the origin and genealogy of the gods.</term> of all ancient peoples were based, as can be perfectly proven, on a primal, incomprehensible, and unnamable **One** $^6)$, which was more like an undivided **One** <note>original Hebrew: אחד (Echad)</note>, **the Being One**, or **the Sole One** $^7)$,
<meta>catchword: than</meta>

---

6) Concerning which one finds excellent material in **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 CE) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose work "On the Theology of Plato" synthesized ancient Greek religious thought.</note> (*On the Theology of Plato*, six books, Hamburg 1618, folio).

7) **The highest of all intellectual things** <note>original Greek: Παντων των νοερων ακροτατον</note>, whose periphery was **the entire unified Intelligible** <note>original Greek: το Νοητον άπαν ηνωμενον</note> and **Formless Form** <note>original Greek: Ειδος αειδος</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the origins of the "Monad" (Unity), arguing that Pythagoras adopted the concept from Egyptian priestly wisdom rather than inventing it. It links this "primal One" to the fundamental structure of all ancient religious systems and Neoplatonic philosophy.</summary>

12) Thus **Plato** speaks in one of his letters to **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius II, the ruler of Syracuse, to whom Plato wrote several letters regarding philosophy and governance.</note> of the **First, Second, and Third** of the **Primary Nature** <note>original Greek: *Prōton, deuteron kai triton tēs te prōta Physeōs*.</note>. **Dionysius** had complained that he could not understand at all what had been told to him regarding the **first cause** <note>original: *Grundursache*</note> of all things. This enigmatic explanation consists of the following words: **"All things are around the King of All, and all things are for His sake, and He is the cause of all beautiful things; and a second is around the second things, and a third is around the third things."** <note>original Greek: *peri ton Pantōn basilea pant’ esti, kai ekeine heneka panta, kai ekeino aition hapantōn tōn kalōn; deuteron de, peri ta deutera; kai triton, peri ta trita.* This famous passage from Plato’s Second Letter was often cited by later thinkers to prove he understood the Trinity.</note> Even if there is not actually talk here of the **Supreme Crown** <note>original Latin: *Corona suprema*; referring to Keter, the highest sphere in the Jewish Kabbalah.</note> of the Kabbalists, nor of the **Holy Trinity** <note>original Latin: *Ternarius sanctus*</note> of the theosophists, the **Platonic** riddle nevertheless stands in some connection with them. The expert, however, easily sees that **Plato** must have understood something more than what he says.

## On the Section concerning Humanity.

"For one might truly say that philosophy is the initiation into the truly perfect rite and the transmission of the mysteries of truly existing things <note>original Greek: Και γαρ αυ την Φιλοσοφίαν μυησιν φαίη τις αν αληθως τελετης, και των οντων ως αληθως μυστηριων παραδοσιν</note>. There are five parts to initiation: the first is the **purification** <note>original Greek: καθαρμος (katharmos)</note>; — — — after the purification, the second is the **transmission of the rite** <note>original Greek: της τελετης παραδοσις</note>; the third is named **contemplation** <note>original Greek: εποπτεια (epopteia)—the highest stage of initiation where the initiate "sees" the sacred truths</note>; the fourth, which is indeed the end of contemplation, is the binding and the placing of crowns <note>original Greek: αναδε σις και στεμματων επιθεσις</note>, so that one is able to transmit to others the rites which one has received; — — and the fifth, which results from these, is **happiness** <note>original Greek: ευδαιμονια (eudaimonia)</note> based on friendship with God and dwelling with the gods. In the same way, there is also the transmission of political discourses <note>original Greek: πολιτικων λογων (politikon logon)</note>; the first part has a certain purification, etc." See Theon of Smyrna, in the cited work, pages 18, 19.

According to this teaching, the purpose of all religion is to promote the <term>communion of the divine with the human</term> <note>original Latin: *Commercium divinorum cum humanis*</note>, a need which man feels most deeply. Therefore, it is rightly concluded that religion has been just as natural as it was necessary for man at all times, whether one views it from his side as an act of homage, or from the side of the Most High as an act of condescension <note>In a theological sense, "condescension" refers to God's willingness to "step down" or accommodate Himself to human understanding.</note>.

It is therefore also as old as man and will remain with him. And although there is only one true religion, this unity does not exclude a variety of means through which its purpose can be achieved.

According to this well-applied principle of true tolerance—which distances itself as much from a soulless jumble of beliefs as it does from that anxious mania for condemnation and exclusive partiality—the article <term>on the idolatry of the nations</term> <note>original Latin: *de idololatria gentium*</note> takes on a completely different appearance.

When speaking of the relative value of a religion, one should, I believe, investigate the following questions above all: How do a people seek God? By what means do they believe they will find Him?

### I.

## General Principle of the Sciences.

What is said in ***Of Errors etc.*** <note>Refers to *Des erreurs et de la vérité* (Of Errors and Truth), published in 1775 by the "Unknown Philosopher" Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin.</note> regarding a general principle of all sciences seems just as dark as it is ambiguous. **Objectively**, I would know of no such thing—namely, no principle in which everything knowable lay in embryonic form and could be developed from it $^{33}$). **Subjectively** however, as it is taken here to some extent, it can mean nothing more than an innate human capacity for all kinds of **intellectual light**, which nonetheless could only ever be considered very relative.

### 2.
## Secret Doctrine of Numbers.

I knew a man who considered it a very ignorant assertion to claim that there was no scale for non-sensory or **virtual magnitudes** <term>virtual magnitudes: In this context, "virtual" (from the Latin *virtus* or "power") refers to non-physical forces or spiritual qualities that possess intensity and effect, even if they lack physical dimensions.</term>; he believed, rather, that numbers could be used for this purpose—if not more usefully, then certainly as usefully as for determining sensory quantities. From the examples provided thus far, it is clear that our own system of numerical characteristics is connected to a much older one. Much more could be said about this if the authentic and complete theory of Pythagoras had been preserved. Indeed, I am convinced that Pythagoras was not the inventor of his cosmological theory of numbers <term>Zahlenlehre: the philosophical study of the mystical significance of numbers</term>. Rather, like Thales <note>An early Greek philosopher often called the first scientist in the Western tradition</note>, he was guided toward it by the Egyptians, whose sacred numbers of the universe—known as the Hermetic numbers <note>attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note>—have already been discussed. However, the authentic Pythagorean theory lies much closer to the actual source of this type of symbolism than what the later semi-Pythagoreans and Neoplatonists <note>A school of mystical philosophy that flourished in late antiquity, blending Plato's thought with religious elements</note> say about it; their conjectures and explanations can rarely be fully relied upon ⁵⁴).

### 4.

## Language and Writing.

Very few, I believe, will be able to make sense of what our theosophers <term>theosophers: seekers of "divine wisdom," often following mystical or esoteric traditions that search for hidden truths in nature and scripture</term> say regarding a true, original, and universal language and script. It is not just the obscurity and remoteness of the subject—which for most people does not even exist—that makes it extremely difficult for those who can only imagine "language" and "script" in the conventional sense to grasp what these terms mean here. It is also the complete lack of examples, which the authors have deliberately avoided, and the absence of proper clues for finding this unknown original <note>the *Ursprache* or primordial language believed to directly express the nature of things, rather than just using arbitrary symbols</note>. An ordinary reader will only grow more impatient with these grand praises the less he feels equipped to clearly recognize and judge what is meant to be so praiseworthy.

Therefore, if there is any humility toward the Creator, if any reverence and magnification of his works, if any charity toward men and zeal for relieving human miseries, if any love of truth in natural things, and hatred of **Darkness**, and a desire to purify the intellect: men must be asked again and again, that having dismissed for a little while or at least set aside those fleeting and preposterous philosophies — — — — They should approach the unfolding of the **Volume of Creatures** <note>original Latin: "Volumen creaturarum" — often called the "Book of Nature," the idea that the physical world is a text written by God that can be read by science</note> submissively and with a certain veneration, and linger in it, meditate upon it, and, washed clean from opinions and the world, engage with it chastely and with integrity. "The god (or the divine) Thoth
